# blitz-2010-freedom-of-thought-extended-mind
- **URL:** https://scholarship.law.okcu.edu/downloads/d7kcg-2ck33/fulltext.pdf · **Accessed:** 2026-09-16 · **For:** v1 response round, finding (a) "unwitting reinvention of Blitz 2010"
- **Citation:** Marc Jonathan Blitz, "Freedom of Thought for the Extended Mind: Cognitive Enhancement and the Constitution," 2010 Wis. L. Rev. 1049. (Full PDF read; HeinOnline pagination visible in footers. PDF page N = law-review page 1048+N.)
- **What it establishes:** Blitz does argue, from Clark & Chalmers' Otto and from the diary, that First Amendment freedom of thought should protect thinking done with external media and technologies. His test: freedom of thought protects activity that is "(1) the functional equivalent of thought, or (2) a reshaping of the self that does that thinking." The editor's substantive point holds — the diary-to-Otto-to-device analogy is Blitz's. BUT the editor's page cites are off (test is at 1072 not 1073; diary passage at 1069 not 1068–69; brain-chip line at 1070 not 1075), and the article contains NO argument about the state *reading, observing, or surveilling* the extended-mind record. Every harm Blitz analyzes is the state *prohibiting, denying, or taking away* the tool (or forcibly altering the brain). Surveillance/privacy is explicitly parked in other constitutional provisions (Fourth Amendment, Due Process), not developed. The word "surveillance" does not appear in the article body. His framing premise is that private thought was historically "beyond the reach of the state" and that neuroscience changed this by enabling *alteration* — not by enabling reading of externalized records.
- **Key passages:**
  - p. 1051–52: "There was no reason for the law to protect our private, unexpressed thoughts because such internal thoughts were, in any case, beyond the reach of the state." … "The government could not manipulate our minds from the inside; its only way of restricting mental activity was to target the communication or other expression that embodies such activity."
  - p. 1069: Otto "is not using writing to communicate with another person as a 'short cut from mind to mind.' Rather, he is using it as a means of enhancing his own thinking. Nonetheless, courts protect such solitary speech under the First Amendment." … "We can make sense of such protection for the journal, not based only on freedom of speech, but freedom of the thinking that underlies it. It is thus appropriate that, in George Orwell's portrait of a thought-police-dominated dystopia, the protagonist's opening rebellion against thought control begins with an entry in a diary."
  - p. 1069 n.103: cites "Baumgartner v. United States, 322 U.S. 665, 673–74, 676–77 (1944) (rejecting an attempt to use a person's allegedly pro-Nazi private diary entries as a basis for revoking citizenship…)" and Porter v. Ascension Parish Sch. Bd. (drawing made "in the 'privacy of his own home'"). [Note: Baumgartner IS a case about the state using a diary against its author — but Blitz cites it only for the proposition that solitary writing is protected "speech"; he does not build a surveillance argument on it.]
  - p. 1070: "If Otto receives First Amendment protection when he inscribes the information he perceives into a journal, why not give him the same protection when he records it in a brain chip or in chemically-altered neuronal circuits? Moreover, if the government would infringe upon his First Amendment rights by denying him a journal, or forbidding other methods of recording his thoughts, would it also infringe upon the same rights if it forbade him from having a memory chip implanted in the first place…?"
  - p. 1070: "If freedom of thought covers journal writing because it is an extension of one's thought and makes further use or refinement of that thought possible, it should perhaps also insulate from state regulation alterations of one's thinking with neural prosthetics or cognitive-enhancement drugs."
  - p. 1072: "freedom of thought cannot and should not protect all activity that arises from or influences thought, but rather activity that is either (1) the functional equivalent of thought, or (2) a reshaping of the self that does that thinking. Freedom of thought, in other words, entails the freedom to think with certain tools or cultural resources in the outside world or to use similar technologies or resources to change the way that one thinks."
  - p. 1073: "Such extended cognition might include someone's regular and automatic use of a journal or iPhone to recall information that others might summon from elsewhere in their brain."
  - p. 1075: "We would view as a grave infringement of free thought any state measure which prevented us from using our brains to access and store our memories. Why then should we not take a similar view of a measure that crippled Otto's (Alzheimer's-transformed) memory by taking away the memory storage equipment that he uses…?"
  - p. 1101 (the only place privacy/search appears in the analysis, and it is a hand-off): "Where a forced drug treatment or medical procedure falls short of that result, it may still run afoul of other constitutional provisions, such as the Due Process Clause's protection of liberty interest or the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable search and seizure."
  - p. 1049 n.4 cites Halliburton, "Letting Katz Out of the Bag: Cognitive Freedom and Fourth Amendment Fidelity" and Richards, "Intellectual Privacy" — the privacy strand is acknowledged only in a footnote.
- **Reliability:** Primary (the article itself, HeinOnline scan). Author is the leading US freedom-of-thought/extended-mind scholar; no independence issue.
- **Relevance to this project:** Establishes that the essay's media-analogy (diary → Otto → technical system) has a direct 2010 precedent and must cite it. Equally establishes the differentiating move available to the author: Blitz's extended-mind freedom of thought is a *prohibition/alteration* right (state may not take away or forbid the tool); the essay's "externalized forum internum" is about *observation/compulsion* (state or platform reading the record). Baumgartner (a diary used as evidence) is sitting in Blitz's own footnote as the seed of the argument he does not make.
